title: Scaling writes: sharding and partition keys
seriesDescription: How to scale write-heavy systems in an interview: vertical scaling and database choice, sharding and partition keys, vertical partitioning, queues and load shedding, batching, hierarchical aggregation, and the resharding and hot-key deep dives.
description: Spreading writes over servers, how Redis Cluster maps keys, and why the choice of partition key makes or breaks the design.
source: Study notes: the scaling writes pattern

questions.prompt: What does sharding give you for write throughput?

options.text: Writes are spread over several servers, so ten servers can handle roughly ten times the volume.
options.why: Right: if the load spreads evenly.

options.text: Every write is copied to every shard to be safe under normal operating conditions.
options.why: That is replication, not sharding.

options.text: Writes are delayed until a replica confirms them.
options.why: Unrelated to sharding.

options.text: Reads become impossible without a full scan for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Reads still find the shard from the key.

questions.explanation: Hide the shards behind one logical database where possible.

questions.prompt: In Redis Cluster, how does a client know where to send a write?

options.text: It hashes the key to a slot number and looks up which node owns that slot.
options.why: Right: clients cache the slot map.

options.text: It broadcasts the write to every node and keeps the first reply.
options.why: That would waste capacity.

options.text: It asks a load balancer to guess a node.
options.why: The slot decides the node.

options.text: It writes to the node with the lowest id.
options.why: Placement is by key; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Consistent hashing is another common scheme to choose the server.

questions.prompt: What makes a good partition key?

options.text: One that spreads writes evenly, such as a hash of a primary identifier like the user id.
options.why: Right: flat load across shards.

options.text: One with only a few possible values, like country for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: A few values create hot shards.

options.text: One that is the same for every record.
options.why: All data would land on one shard.

options.text: One chosen only for how easy it is to type as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Distribution matters, not typing.

questions.explanation: Aim to minimise the variance of writes per shard.

questions.prompt: Why is country a poor shard key for a global user base?

options.text: Heavily populated countries overload their shard while small ones sit idle.
options.why: Right: uneven distribution.

options.text: Country names are too long to hash.
options.why: Length is irrelevant; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Countries change every day, so keys are unstable in a typical production setup.
options.why: They do not; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: It requires a different database type for each country without any extra configuration.
options.why: It does not; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: The graph of writes per shard should be flat.

questions.prompt: Which question should you ask about a candidate partition key besides write balance?

options.text: How many shards does a typical request hit, and how often does it happen?
options.why: Right: avoid scatter-gather on hot paths.

options.text: How long is the key in bytes? as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Not the main concern; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Which team named the column?
options.why: Irrelevant; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: How many tables exist in the schema? for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Not related to the key choice.

questions.explanation: Spreading writes evenly is no good if every read must visit every shard.

questions.prompt: True or false: hashing a primary identifier such as userId or postId is a common way to get an even spread across shards.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: it is the usual approach.

options.text: False
options.why: It is in fact the usual way to spread load.

questions.explanation: A hash of a high-cardinality id spreads records evenly and gives a simple lookup.

questions.prompt: An interviewer says "you said sharding, how does a client find the right shard?" What is a good answer?

options.text: Hash the partition key to a slot or ring position, and look up the owning server, caching the map.
options.why: Right: slots, consistent hashing or virtual nodes.

options.text: The application tries every shard until one answers for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: That is a scatter on every request.

options.text: The database figures it out and never tells the client without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
options.why: Clients or a router need the mapping.

options.text: Use a random shard and retry on failure.
options.why: Placement must be deterministic.

questions.explanation: Be ready to discuss consistent hashing, virtual nodes and slot assignment.

questions.prompt: How should you arrange your "fastest" data, the most read and written?

options.text: Spread reads and writes evenly while grouping commonly accessed data together.
options.why: Right: balance load and locality.

options.text: Put all of it on a single shard for simplicity without any extra configuration.
options.why: That creates a bottleneck.

options.text: Scatter related items across all shards on purpose as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: That multiplies cross-shard reads.

options.text: Keep it only in client memory.
options.why: That is not durable or shared.

questions.explanation: Expect a discussion with the interviewer on physical layout.
